**In Defense of Getting Lost**

Every child knows two kinds of lost. There is the bad kind—the supermarket aisle where your mother's face has vanished, the sudden cold geometry of adult legs moving past—and there is the other kind, found at the end of a creek followed behind the houses until the backyards give way to trees and you look up and cannot name any street at all. The first kind teaches caution. The second, if you are lucky enough to survive it unremarked, teaches something stranger: that the world continues past the edge of the map you were handed, that you can find your way home, and that not knowing—briefly, safely endured—is nearer to wonder than to terror.

Then we grow up and set about losing nothing. We carry objects that know where we are to within a few meters, that announce turns before we need them, that can summon a picture of any corner of any city on earth. This is presented to us as freedom, and in many ways it is. But notice what else it is: the end of a certain education. For nearly all of human history, every journey contained a small wilderness of uncertainty. You might take a wrong turn. You might misjudge the distance. You might arrive somewhere you did not intend and have to negotiate with reality to get where you were going. That negotiation was a skill, and like all skills it was built through use.

People have always sensed this, which is why the great traditions of walking are also traditions of deliberate confusion. The flâneurs of nineteenth-century Paris strolled without destination precisely because destination was the enemy of seeing. The Situationists later gave the practice a name—the dérive, the drift—and treated it as a serious method, a way of letting the city speak instead of merely using it. Pilgrims walked for months toward distant shrines, but everyone understood the shrine was half the point; the other half was the long corridor of days in which a traveler could become someone slightly different than the one who set out. Even Thoreau admitted he sometimes stayed out past dark because his walks had carried him somewhere unplanned—and he suspected, rightly, that the best part of his day happened while lost.

What the blue dot took from us was not safety—we are safer—but the productive friction of being briefly wrong. Watch people navigate now: the phone speaks, the body obeys, and the mind is free to drift elsewhere entirely. We arrive having gone nowhere in the sense that matters. Compare this to navigating by folded paper map, an instrument that required you to hold the whole territory in your head at once—to know the museum is behind you and the river ahead, that north hangs over your left shoulder. With one, you built a model of the city inside yourself. You became a little map. And when a closed road forced you into unfamiliar blocks, you had the resources to improvise, and the improvisation left marks. People remember the streets they got lost in. Nobody remembers the streets they were routed through.

Something notable also happens in the mind during disorientation. When you know exactly where you are and what comes next, attention relaxes into shorthand; the world arrives pre-labeled. But when you are lost, attention snaps open. Every façade becomes information. Every signpost is read with the urgency of scripture. Researchers studying wayfinding find that people form richer memories of places navigated unaided, and anyone learning a new city knows it is true at the level of feeling: the streets you struggled through are the ones you own. Disorientation is a powerful teacher precisely because it refuses to summarize. It makes you do the work of orienting yourself, and the work is the lesson.

None of this needs to stay literal. We get lost in books, in arguments, in other people's troubles, in a problem of our own that swallows an afternoon. Intellectual lostness wears the same double face as the geographic kind: frustration braided with fascination. The mathematician stuck on a proof, the writer staring at a sentence that won't behave, the child dismantling a clock—they are all off the map, doing what experts call exploration when it succeeds and flailing when it doesn't. But every map of a field worth caring about was drawn by people willing to flail. Certainty is comfortable, and comfort is where curiosity goes to die. If you always know exactly where you stand in an idea, you are probably standing at its entrance, reading the plaque.

Still, it matters to distinguish getting lost from mere aimlessness, because they are not the same. Drifting can be lovely, but true lostness requires that you cared where you were going—that there was a destination, a plan, a self you expected to keep intact—and that reality disagreed. Lostness is what happens to intention when it collides with the world. This is why the word carries such weight beyond geography: people describe themselves as lost after a failure, a move, a heartbreak. We treat that state as purely negative, yet it is often the precondition for the next version of a life. You cannot reorient until you admit you are facing the wrong way. The admission hurts. It is also, quietly, hopeful—it means movement is still possible.

So consider, sometime soon, a small experiment. Leave the phone in your pocket—not off, just unprompted—and choose a direction you've never taken out of your own neighborhood, or walk your usual route backward, or follow the sound of water. Expect the flicker of anxiety; let it pass through you like weather. Notice how sharply the world arranges itself around your uncertainty, how much there is to see once seeing becomes necessary. Then find your way home by whatever means remain: the angle of the sun, the slope of the land, the kindness of a stranger. You will arrive late, slightly rumpled, with dirt on your shoes and a story nobody asked for. And for an hour or so, you will have been the author of your own route again—present in the world, finally, because you were lost enough to truly pay attention.

Psychologists studying wayfinding find that people form richer memories of places navigated without assistance, and anyone who has ever tried to learn a new city knows it is true at the level of feeling: the streets you struggled through are the ones you own. Disorientation, it turns out, is a powerful teacher precisely because it refuses to summarize. It makes you do the work of orientation yourself, and the work is the lesson.

(~140)

None of this needs to stay literal. We get lost in books, in arguments, in other people's problems, in a problem of our own that swallows an afternoon. Intellectual lostness has the same double face as geographic lostness: frustration braided with fascination. The mathematician stuck on a proof, the writer staring at a sentence that won't behave, the child taking apart a clock—they are all off the map, doing the thing experts call "exploration" when it succeeds and "flailing" when it doesn't. But the map of any field worth caring about was drawn by people willing to flail. Certainty is comfortable, and comfort is where curiosity goes to die. If you always know where you are in an idea, you are probably standing at its entrance, reading the plaque.

(~140)

It matters, though, to distinguish getting lost from simply wandering without commitment, because they are not the same. Aimlessness can be lovely, but true lostness requires that you cared where you were going—that there was a destination, a plan, a self you expected to remain intact—and that reality disagreed. Lostness is what happens to intention when it meets the world. This is why the word carries such freight beyond geography: people describe themselves as lost after a failure, a move, a heartbreak, a diagnosis. And though we treat that state as purely negative, it is often the precondition for the next version of a life. You cannot reorient until you admit you are facing the wrong way. The admission hurts. It is also, quietly, hopeful—it means movement is still possible.

(~140)

So consider, sometime soon, a small experiment. Leave the phone in your pocket—not off, just unprompted—and pick a direction you've never taken out of your neighborhood, or take your usual route backward, or follow the sound of water. Expect the flicker of anxiety; let it pass through you like weather. Notice how sharply the world arranges itself around your uncertainty, how much there is to see once seeing becomes necessary. Then find your way home by whatever means remain: the angle of the sun, the slope of the land, the kindness of a stranger. You will arrive late, slightly rumpled, with dirt on your shoes and a story no one asked for.

You will also, briefly, have been the author of your own route again—which is to say, for an hour or so, you will have been fully present in the world, lost enough to finally pay attention.

(~160)
